**567 VA OIG recommendations are open** in this dataset. **OIG's own dashboard shows 586.** The data is as of **November 4, 2026**, which is 13 days old, so it isn't stale.

**Why the two numbers differ:** On November 4, 2026 the dataset was checked row by row against OIG's public pages, and it passed. Every open recommendation OIG lists is in the data, and nothing extra is. The 19-item gap comes from 19 blank rows on OIG's pages that have no recommendation details. OIG's total of 586 counts them, but they can't be matched to specific recommendations. The difference is within the accepted tolerance. Source: [OIG data dashboard](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/data-dashboard).

**How old the open recommendations are**

By OIG's count of 586:
- Under 1 year: 409
- 1 to 5 years: 160
- Over 5 years: 17

These add up to OIG's 586, not to this dataset's 567.

By the year the report was published, using the 567 in this dataset (189 reports in total):

| Year | Open recommendations | Reports |
|---|---|---|
| 2018 | 1 | 1 |
| 2021 | 18 | 9 |
| 2022 | 13 | 7 |
| 2023 | 24 | 8 |
| 2024 | 24 | 14 |
| 2025 | 118 | 47 |
| 2026 | 369 | 103 |

About two-thirds of the open items come from 2026 reports. That's expected, because new recommendations stay open while VA works on them. It doesn't by itself mean things are getting worse. A pile-up in recent years can reflect how many reports OIG published, changes in how inspections are done, or where OIG focused, as well as how long fixes take. Closure dates aren't available for these open items, so this data can't say how long they will take to close.

**For context:** of the 15,649 recommendations in the dataset, 14,925 were closed as implemented and 157 were closed as not implemented. OIG's total is 15,778; the 129-item difference is also within tolerance.

These are totals across all reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's [recommendations page](https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all) and data dashboard. I can break the open items down by office (VHA, VBA, OIT, and others), topic, state, or facility if that would help.

In 2026, OIG's Healthcare Facility Inspection reports made **148 recommendations**, and **80 of them are still open**.

The data runs through **November 4, 2026**, 13 days ago, so it's current. Reports published later in 2026 aren't counted.

| | Count |
|---|---|
| Reports published in 2026 | 61 |
| Recommendations made | 148 |
| Still open | 80 (54%), across 31 reports |
| Closed as implemented | 68 |
| Closed as not implemented | 0 |

**Notes from the data:**
- **How the 61 reports are counted:** The total includes all reports published in the program in 2026, even ones with no recommendations. The 31 reports with open items count only reports that have at least one open recommendation.
- **Closures on day one:** The median time to close is 0 days. That means at least half of the 68 closed recommendations were closed the day the report came out, presumably because the facility fixed the problem before publication. It doesn't mean recommendations usually close that fast.
- **No dates for open items:** The 80 open recommendations have no closure dates, so there's no way to say from this data how long they will take to close.
- **OIG's count is a little higher:** Across all OIG reports, OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both. The gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages. That could mean the 80 here is slightly low, though the data doesn't say whether any of those rows are from 2026 facility inspections.
- **Why so many are open:** Many of these reports came out only months ago, so a high share of open items is expected. It doesn't by itself show slow follow-through.
- **Comparing with other years:** A change in counts can mean conditions changed, or that inspection methods, the number of reports, or OIG's focus changed.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's recommendations page (https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all). I can list the open recommendations or break them down by state or topic.

OIG issued the most recommendations in **2015: 1,914**, spread across 396 reports. Almost all of them are closed: 1,903 were implemented and 11 were closed without being implemented.

The next highest years were 2014 with 1,670 and 2020 with 1,211. In the years since, the yearly total has been between about 600 and 1,150.

**Notes:**
- **Data date:** The data is current as of 2026-11-04, which was 13 days old when I checked, so it isn't stale. The 2026 figure of 631 covers only part of the year.
- **Gaps before 2012:** This data has almost no recommendations before 2012, even though OIG published reports in those years. The yearly counts only work as a comparison from 2012 onward, and 2015 is the peak in this data, not necessarily in OIG's whole history.
- **Small gap from OIG's total:** This data has 15,649 recommendations, while OIG's own total is 15,778, a difference of 129. That gap is within tolerance and is very unlikely to change which year is the peak.
- **How to read the trend:** A change in the yearly count can mean more than one thing. A drop after 2015 could mean fewer problems were found. It could also mean OIG published fewer reports, changed how it inspects, or shifted its attention. 2015 also had the most reports of any year, which accounts for part of its high total.
- **Open count:** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check matched them; the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

These figures are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. They come from OIG's public recommendations list at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

run.answer:
**No, not by this measure.** The number of reports with a recommendation mentioning suicide dropped sharply from 2024 to 2025. But most of that drop comes from OIG retiring one inspection program, so it doesn't show that OIG cares less about suicide prevention.

The data is current as of 4 November 2026 (13 days old, not stale).

## The counts
Reports with at least one recommendation containing "suicide":

| Year | Reports | Matching recommendations | All reports with recommendations | Share of reports |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024 | **56** | 98 (of 878) | 155 | about 36% |
| 2025 | **11** | 19 (of 775) | 132 | about 8% |

Total recommendations fell only about 12%, while the suicide-mention count fell about 80%. So the drop isn't just OIG publishing less.

## What explains the drop
- **A program change.** In 2024, 55 of the 98 matching recommendations came from the Comprehensive Healthcare Inspection Program. That program produced 221 recommendations in 2024 and none in 2025. Its replacement, the Healthcare Facility Inspection program, made 167 recommendations in 2025, and none of them contained the keyword.
- **Without that program, the drop is much smaller.** Other report types went from about 43 matching recommendations in 2024 to 19 in 2025. In 2025 the matches came from Mental Health Inspections (9), Vet Center Inspections (5), National Healthcare Reviews (3) and Hotline Inspections (2).
- **The count has always jumped around.** Matching reports by year: 2016: 35, 2017: 6, 2020: 23, 2021: 34, 2022: 10, 2023: 32, 2024: 56, 2025: 11, 2026 so far: 10. 2024 was the highest year on record, not a normal level, so comparing against it makes any later year look like a fall.

## What these counts can show
- How often OIG's recommendations explicitly use the word "suicide," and in which kinds of reports.
- That this fell from 2024 to 2025, largely because of how OIG's inspections are set up.

## What they cannot show
- **Whether suicide prevention matters more or less to OIG.** A falling count can mean things improved. It can also mean inspection protocols, report volume or OIG's focus changed. The program switch is strong evidence of the second explanation here, but the data can't settle it.
- **Whether VA's suicide-prevention care got better or worse.** A recommendation means OIG found a gap at one place and time. It doesn't measure quality.
- **Everything about suicide prevention.** The search finds only the word itself. Recommendations about related work in other words, such as safety plans, lethal-means counseling or high-risk flags, are missed. Searching "suicidal" gave the same results as "suicide," which suggests the search matches word variants, but I can't confirm that. Topic tags would be no fuller: OIG tagged only about a quarter of reports.
- **The full story of the 2025 reports.** Some are still open: 6 of the 19 recommendations are unresolved. That affects whether they're open or closed, not the counts.

## Notes from the data source
- OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations and this data has 567. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both; the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.
- Target dates: the facility sets its own target date. OIG's closure date appears to record when it reviewed the evidence, which can be months after the work was done. A late closure doesn't prove a missed commitment.

**The median is 179 days.** That figure covers VBA recommendations that OIG has closed, counted from when the report was published to when OIG marked the recommendation closed. The data is current as of **2026-11-04** (13 days old, not stale).

**The numbers (VBA)**
- **Median:** 179 days.
- **Middle half of closures:** 134 to 312.5 days. A quarter closed in under about 4½ months, and a quarter took more than about 10 months.
- **Size of the measurement:** 914 closed recommendations. VBA has 966 recommendations in total: 923 closed (897 implemented, 26 not implemented, a 2.8% not-implemented rate) and 43 still open.
- **Still open:** the open items have a median age of 161 days. 17 have been open more than a year, and the oldest is 1,567 days old (about 4.3 years).

**What the median measures, and what it doesn't**
- **It measures when OIG closed the recommendation, not when VBA finished the work.** The closure date appears to be when OIG closed the recommendation after reviewing VBA's evidence, which can come months after the work was done. So 179 days is closer to "time until OIG accepted the fix" than "time VBA took to fix it."
- **It doesn't show whether VBA met its own deadlines.** A target date is the agency's own estimate. Closing after the target, or staying open past it, doesn't show that VBA missed its commitment.
- **Only closed recommendations count.** The 43 open items aren't included. Of the 923 closed, 9 have no closure date and are left out, which is why the measurement covers 914. Across all of OIG's data, about 6% of closed recommendations, mostly from 2013–2016, show no closure date on OIG's site.
- **Same-day closures lower the median.** 110 VBA recommendations were closed the day the report came out, probably because the problem was fixed before publication. They count as 0 days. In a group this large they shift the median a little rather than collapsing it.
- **Some recommendations name more than one office.** Those count for each office, so filtering for VBA also returned small groups shared with other offices: OIT (11 recommendations, median 330 days) and VHA (5, median 71). Those overlap with the VBA count, so don't add them to it.

**Data note:** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations across all offices, while this data has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both, and the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

These are totals across many reports, so no single report is the source. The underlying data comes from OIG's recommendations listing at https://www.vaoig.gov/recommendations-all.

OIG made **two recommendations** in report 25-00193-155. The facility **agreed** with the one about keeping the environment clean and safe and set a **target date of January 29, 2027**.

**Report:** *Healthcare Facility Inspection of the VA El Paso Healthcare System in Texas*, published July 16, 2026. Report 25-00193-155, https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system ([PDF](https://www.vaoig.gov/sites/default/files/reports/2026-07/vaoig-25-00193-155_final.pdf))

**The two recommendations:**
1. **Environment of care:** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment."
2. **Primary care:** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." The facility agreed with this one too, with a target date of December 31, 2026.

**The facility's plan for recommendation 1 (report page 12):**
- **Daily cleaning:** Environmental Management Services staff inspect and clean all areas at least once a day. Restroom cleaning is recorded on logs posted on the doors, and signs give a number to call if a restroom isn't clean.
- **Busy restrooms:** A technician is assigned to check high-traffic public restrooms throughout each business day.
- **Procedures and training:** 24 standard operating procedures for cleaning and disinfection are in place, and staff were trained on June 2, 2026. At an all-staff town hall the same day, employees were told their role in keeping the facility clean and safe.
- **Oversight:** The Chief of Environmental Management Services checks cleanliness daily, and the Associate Director inspects it weekly during environment-of-care rounds.

**Status:** Both recommendations were still **open** as of the data date. OIG hasn't closed recommendation 1, so the record can't yet show whether the work was finished by the target date.

**About the data:**
- The data is current as of **November 4, 2026** (13 days old, not stale).
- In this dataset, the facility's response to recommendation 1 also contains other report text, such as findings OIG chose not to make recommendations for. That looks like an extraction error, so I only summarized the part that answers the recommendation. The PDF has the original wording.
- Dataset-wide notice: OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations, while this dataset has 567. A row-by-row check found the same recommendations in both; the difference is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages. This doesn't affect this report.

**The most common recurring finding is about how test results get communicated to patients. El Paso is not in that group.** Data is current as of **2026-11-04** (13 days old, not stale).

## The most common finding

Within the Healthcare Facility Inspection program, the largest cluster by number of reports is **cluster 260**. Its label, quoted from OIG:

> "The Chief of Staff and Associate Director for Patient Care Services develop workflows that describe how each team member participates in the process to communicate test results, in accordance with Veterans Health Administration Directive 1088(1), Communicating Test Results to Providers and Patients."

**How common it is:**
- **It appears in 21 of the 112 inspection reports** in scope, about 19%. Those 21 reports contain 26 recommendations.
- **All 26 are from reports published in 2026.** The earliest is Central Alabama, published January 2026; the latest are Maryland and Phoenix, published October 2026.
- **17 are still open and 9 are closed and implemented.** None were closed as not implemented.
- **The median time to close is 0 days**, based on only 9 closed recommendations. A 0 means those 9 were closed on the day the report came out, so it doesn't show how long fixes usually take.

**This theme is bigger than one cluster.** A related cluster (261), on test-result policy and monitoring whether patients are notified, appears in another **12 of 112 reports** (2025–2026). The two can't simply be added together, because some reports may be in both.

**Limits on what a cluster means:** it groups recommendations with matching or similar wording. That points to a shared issue but doesn't prove a common cause. One theme can also be split across several clusters, so a single cluster isn't a full count of a theme.

## Is the VA El Paso Healthcare System in the group?

**No.** I checked all 26 recommendations in cluster 260, and none are from El Paso (station 756). El Paso's latest inspection made two recommendations, both still open:

- **Recommendation 1:** "Executive leaders ensure staff maintain a clean and safe environment." This is part of a different cluster (270), about keeping the environment clean and safe.
- **Recommendation 2:** "The Medical Center Director ensures providers complete secondary toxic exposure screenings within 30 days." This one isn't part of any cluster.

Source: Report 25-00193-155, https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-va-el-paso-healthcare-system (inspected January 14–16, 2025; published July 16, 2026).

**Other notes:**
- **Next inspection:** this tool estimates around January 2028, based on OIG's roughly three-year cycle counted from the last inspection's end date. That's only an estimate; OIG publishes no schedule.
- **Open findings aren't predictions:** the open items show what is still unresolved, not what OIG will cite next time.
- **Repeat findings:** the tool found none for El Paso. It only compares recommendations that belong to a cluster, and a repeat would mean the same issue was cited again, not that nothing was done in between.
- **VISN label:** El Paso's VISN 17 tag comes from OIG's report tags in VA's former numbering. It may not match El Paso's network under the five networks VA created on July 15, 2026.
- **Open-count mismatch:** OIG's dashboard shows 586 open recommendations overall, while this data has 567. A row-by-row comparison found the same recommendations in both; the gap is 19 blank rows on OIG's pages.

Yes. OIG has cited unlocked or unattended medication carts many times. Most of these findings came from its routine facility inspections between 2012 and 2016, and related findings on unsecured medications still appear in its current inspection program. This data is current as of **November 4, 2026**, 13 days old, so it isn't stale.

## Recommendations about unsecured medication carts
All of these are closed as implemented.

This is the most serious example. OIG found that "some medication carts were unlocked and unattended," and that staff could use one code to unlock carts across the facility. OIG called open access to insulin in carts "concerning" given the unexplained low blood sugar events in the homicide cases.
- **[14-02396-212](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/healthcare-inspection-alleged-medication-cart-deficiencies)**, Atlanta, Jul 2014. This complaint-driven inspection was about carts that didn't work properly and unsafe ways of giving medications.
- **[16-00549-302](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/comprehensive-healthcare-inspection-program/clinical-assessment-program-review-aleda-e-lutz)**, Saginaw, Jul 2017. OIG recommended repairing broken carts or taking them out of service.
- **Unlocked code (emergency) carts:** Dayton, [18-01275-89](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/quality-care-issues-community-living-center-and-emergency), and Biloxi, [18-00808-186](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/hotline-healthcare-inspection/mismanagement-resuscitation-and-other-concerns-gulf-coast).

## Current inspection program (2024 onward)
Recent findings are worded more broadly, as securing medications "from unauthorized access":
- **Minneapolis**, [24-03416-237](https://www.vaoig.gov/reports/healthcare-facility-inspection/healthcare-facility-inspection-minneapolis-va-health-care), Nov 2025. **Still open**, with a target date of August 2026.
